title: Who I Am
overview: This unit gives you the sentences you need before any other sentence: who you are, how old you are, where you live, and how to say it to a person who is waiting for an answer. It teaches the single most useful verb in English — am, is, are — and the small words that go with it. By the end you can introduce yourself, give your details to someone filling in a form, and say a date out loud without stopping to think.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. It explains all five patterns.
Open Patterns. Each card has one done for you before you try the rest.
Learn the words. There are twenty-nine, in five small groups.
Read the three texts aloud. One of them is an appointment card, and you will need to read one of those.
Do the Practice. Every exercise has its answer — try first, then check.
Record yourself saying your own details, and play it back.
Take the quiz, then mark where you are in My progress.
lectureScript:
In the last unit you worked on sound. Now you need sentences, and we start with the most useful verb in English.
That verb is be. In the present it has three forms: am, is, are. You will use it more than any other verb, in every conversation you ever have.
Here is the whole thing. I am. You are. He is. She is. It is. We are. They are.
That is it. Three forms, seven pronouns. Learn which goes with which and a very large part of basic English is already working.
Am goes with I, and only with I. Nothing else in the language uses am.
Is goes with he, she and it — one person or one thing.
Are goes with you, we and they — and also with you when you mean one person. English does not have a separate word for one you and many you. The same word does both jobs.
Now, why does this matter so much? Because in many languages you do not need a word here at all. You can say something like: I teacher. She tired. He from Egypt. Those are complete, correct sentences in plenty of languages. In English they are not. English needs the verb. I am a teacher. She is tired. He is from Egypt. If you leave it out, people will still understand you — but it is the single most noticeable thing about beginner English, and it is easy to fix.
Next: the pronouns themselves. I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Two things to know. First, I is always a capital letter, anywhere in the sentence — English does this with no other word. Second, English uses he and she for people, and it for everything that is not a person. A car is it. A city is it. A dog is usually it. Get that wrong and it sounds strange rather than wrong, but it is worth knowing.
Third pattern: my, your, his, her. These say who something belongs to. My name. Your address. His phone. Her office. Notice they come before the thing, never after it, and notice that the word does not change when the thing is plural. My name, my names. My child, my children. It stays my.
And one thing that catches people: his and her follow the owner, not the thing owned. If the phone belongs to a man, it is his phone. If it belongs to a woman, it is her phone. The phone itself has nothing to do with it.
Fourth: numbers and age. English says how old are you, not how many years have you. And the answer is I am thirty. Not I have thirty. Again, this is a place where many languages use a different verb, and English uses be.
Fifth: the calendar. Days, months, dates. Two things you need immediately. Days and months always take a capital letter in English — Monday, January, never monday or january. And dates are said differently from how they are written. You write the fourteenth of March, or 14 March, and you say the fourteenth of March. The word the and the word of are there when you say it, even when they are not written down.
That is five patterns. Go to Patterns, work through the cards, and do the practice on each one before you move to the next.

outcomes.outcome: Use am, is and are correctly with each subject pronoun, in statements, questions and negatives.
outcomes.evidence: Patterns 1 practice self-checked; Practice 1 completed with eight or more of ten correct; Speaking 1 recording.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say who I am and where I am from in full sentences, using am, is or are.

outcomes.outcome: Choose the right subject pronoun for a person or a thing, and match it to the right form of be.
outcomes.evidence: Practice 2 pronoun replacement, ten items; Quiz items 2 and 6.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can see who a sentence is about and choose he, she, it or they correctly.

outcomes.outcome: Show what belongs to whom using my, your, his and her, placed before the noun.
outcomes.evidence: Patterns 3 practice; Writing 2, in which every possessive is underlined and checked.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write my name, your address, his phone and her office without mixing them up.

outcomes.outcome: Say and write numbers to one hundred, ask someone's age, and give your own.
outcomes.evidence: Practice 4 number dictation, self-marked; Speaking 3 recording of the age exchange.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can ask how old someone is and answer when someone asks me.

outcomes.outcome: Read and say a date, and write days and months with the capital letter English requires.
outcomes.evidence: Practice 5 dates, ten items; the appointment card in Reading 3 read correctly, including the date.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can read a date on a card and say it out loud correctly.

outcomes.outcome: Greet someone, respond to a greeting, and close a short exchange politely.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 5 recording of the full six-turn exchange; Practice 6 matching.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can start a short conversation with someone I do not know, and end it politely.

words.meaning: What people call you.
practice: I did not hear your name.
Her name is on the card.
words.tutor: Say your name three ways: just the name, then My name is…, then a full introduction. Ask the tutor which sounded most natural.

words.meaning: Your family name, the one you share with your family.
words.example: Please write your surname in capital letters.
practice: My surname is difficult to spell.
The form asks for your surname.
words.tutor: Spell your surname out loud, letter by letter. Ask the tutor to write it back and check it matches.

words.meaning: Where you live: the street, the number and the town.
practice: Write your address on the form.
The letter went to my old address.
words.tutor: Say an address out loud — you may invent one. Ask the tutor to repeat it back to you.

words.meaning: How many years old you are.
words.example: The form asks for your age.
practice: Children under this age pay nothing.
She did not want to give her age.
Please write your age in the box.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor two ways: What is your age, and How old are you. Ask which one people say more.

words.meaning: The word for coming into the world; used to say when or where your life started.
practice: She was born in the same town.
He was born on the fourteenth.
The form asks where you were born.
words.tutor: Say when you were born and where. You may change the details if you prefer.

words.meaning: The word that shows where you started or where you come from.
words.example: I am from a small town.
practice: They are from the same place.
This letter is from the office.
words.tutor: Answer Where are you from three times, each time with a different amount of detail.

words.meaning: An adult male person. More than one: men.
words.example: The man at the desk will help you.
practice: Ask the man in the blue shirt.
words.tutor: Say the sentence with man, then with men. Ask the tutor whether it heard one person or more.

words.meaning: An adult female person. More than one: women.
words.example: The woman at the desk is helpful.
practice: Three women are in the office.
Ask the woman by the door.
words.tutor: Woman and women are said differently even though the spelling barely changes. Say both to the tutor.

words.meaning: A person you like and know well, who is not family.
words.example: My friend is waiting for me.
practice: She is a friend from work.
He is not a friend, he is a neighbour.
A friend gave me this address.
words.tutor: Describe one friend in three sentences using is. You may invent the person.

words.meaning: A person who lives near you.
practice: She is my neighbour, not my friend.
Ask your neighbour about the bins.
A neighbour helped me with the form.
words.tutor: Say two sentences: one about a neighbour and one about a friend. Ask the tutor to say what the difference is.

words.meaning: A person you work with.
words.example: A colleague showed me the way.
practice: My colleagues are from many places.
He is a colleague, not my manager.
Ask a colleague if you are not sure.
She is a colleague from the other office.
words.tutor: Introduce a colleague in one sentence, then say what they do in a second.

words.meaning: The people you are related to.
practice: She has family in another town.
This is a photo of my family.
words.tutor: Say three sentences about a family — yours or an invented one. Use is at least twice.

words.meaning: A word or sign for how many, such as 3 or 40.
practice: The number is on the card.
Write the number in the box.
words.tutor: Say a phone number out loud, in groups of two or three digits. Ask the tutor to repeat it back.

words.meaning: Having lived or existed for a long time; also used to say your age.
practice: She is two years older than me.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor how old it is, then answer the same question about yourself. You may invent the number.

words.meaning: Not having lived long; the opposite of old.
words.example: She is very young for this job.
practice: The class is for young children.
He looks younger than he is.
I was young when I came here.
words.tutor: Say one sentence with young and one with old about the same person.

words.meaning: Twelve months.
words.example: I have been here for one year.
practice: Every year it is the same.
words.tutor: Say how long you have been somewhere, using year or years. Check you added the s for more than one.

words.meaning: The number 100.
words.example: There are about a hundred people here.
practice: The form has a hundred questions.
A hundred years is a long time.
words.tutor: English says a hundred or one hundred, never just hundred. Say all three and hear which sounds wrong.

words.meaning: One of the seven parts of a week.
words.example: Which day is best for you?
practice: The office is closed on that day.
Come on any day this week.
words.tutor: Say the seven days of the week out loud. Ask the tutor whether each one started with a capital sound.

words.meaning: Seven days.
practice: The course is four weeks long.
I work five days a week.
words.tutor: Say what you will do next week in three sentences.

words.meaning: The day, month and year that something happens.
practice: Write the date at the top.
The date is on your card.
We agreed a date for the meeting.
words.tutor: Say today's date out loud twice, in the two orders English allows. Ask the tutor which it prefers.

words.meaning: This day, the one happening now.
words.tutor: Say three things about today. Use is in each one.

words.meaning: The day after today.
words.tutor: Say what you will do tomorrow, then what you did today. Notice which one is harder.

words.meaning: The day each year when you remember the day you were born.
practice: Her birthday is on the ninth.
The form asks for your date of birth, not your birthday.
words.tutor: Say your birthday two ways: the month only, then the full date. You may change it if you prefer.

words.meaning: The word you say when you meet someone or answer the phone.
practice: Hello — are you the new student?
Hello, can you help me, please?
He did not even say hello.
words.tutor: Say hello and then introduce yourself, without stopping between the two.

words.meaning: The word you say when you leave.
practice: It is time to say goodbye.
words.tutor: End a short conversation with the tutor properly: thank it, say goodbye, and wait for the reply.

words.meaning: The word you add to a request to make it polite.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three things, each time with please. Then ask once without it and notice the difference.

words.meaning: The word you say when you have done something wrong, or when you did not hear.
words.example: Sorry — I did not hear you.
practice: Sorry, can you say that again?
words.tutor: Use sorry two different ways: once as an apology, once to ask for a repeat.

words.meaning: Used in excuse me, to get someone's attention politely or to pass by them.
words.example: Excuse me, is this the right office?
practice: Excuse me — can I get past?
Excuse me, what time is it?
Excuse me, I have a question.
words.tutor: Start three different questions with excuse me. Ask the tutor which sounded most polite.

words.meaning: Used to greet someone arriving, and in you are welcome after a thank you.
words.tutor: Thank the tutor for something and listen to how it replies. Then swap roles.

readings.title: Three People Say Who They Are
readings.passage:
Hello. My name is Ana. My surname is Costa. I am thirty-four years old and I am from a small town in the north. I live here now, in Park Road. I am a nurse, but I am not working at the moment — I am studying.
Hello. I am Tomas. I am twenty-nine. I am not from here; my family is in another country. My wife is here with me and our daughter is at school. She is six. I am a driver.
Good morning. My name is Priya Sharma. Sharma is my surname. I am forty-one. I am from a city, but my parents are from a village two hours away. I am an engineer. My English is not good yet, but it is better than last year.
Read these three again and notice one thing. Every single sentence has am, is or are in it. Not one of them can be said without it.

readings.title: Which Name Goes in Which Box?
readings.passage:
English forms ask for your name in two parts, and they do not always use the same words for them.
The part you share with your family may be called surname, family name, or last name. All three mean the same thing.
The part that is only yours may be called first name, given name, or forename. Again, all the same thing.
Be careful with first name and last name. They do not mean the first and last name you say — they mean the position on an English form. If you normally say your family name first, an English form will still want it in the surname box.
Some forms ask for middle name. If you do not have one, write NONE or leave it empty. It is not a problem.
One more thing. Many forms say write in capital letters. This is not about being polite. Handwriting is hard to read, and a name written badly goes into a computer wrongly, and then the letter never arrives.
If you are not sure which box is which, look for the word surname or family name. That box is always the family part, whatever the rest of the form calls it.

readings.title: Appointment Card
readings.setting: The card you are given after making an appointment.
readings.passage:
HEALTH CENTRE — APPOINTMENT CARD

Name:        A. COSTA
Patient no.: 4471 993

Appointment: Tuesday 14 March
Time:        09:40
With:        Dr Bennett, Room 3

Please arrive 10 minutes before your appointment time.
Bring this card and a list of any medicine you take.

If you cannot come, telephone 0300 118 4422 at least
24 hours before. There is no charge if you telephone.

Next appointment: ____ / ____ / ________

comprehension.q: How old is Ana, and where is she from?
comprehension.a: She is thirty-four, and she is from a small town in the north.
comprehension.why: Both details are in her first two sentences. Notice that both use is.

comprehension.q: Tomas says I am not from here. Who else is not from where they live now?
comprehension.a: Nobody exactly, but Priya's parents are from a village two hours away, while she is from a city.
comprehension.why: This needs care: Priya herself is from the city she lives in — it is her parents who are from somewhere else.

comprehension.q: What is the one thing the text asks you to notice about all three introductions?
comprehension.a: Every sentence uses am, is or are, and none of them work without it.
comprehension.why: The last two lines say so directly. It is the point of the whole text.

comprehension.q: Priya says my English is not good yet, but it is better than last year. What does the word yet tell you?
comprehension.a: That she expects it to get better — she is talking about now, not about always.
comprehension.why: This is an inference. Yet turns a negative into a temporary one, which is why it is worth noticing so early.

comprehension.q: Name three different words an English form might use for your family name.
comprehension.a: Surname, family name, and last name.
comprehension.why: The second paragraph lists all three and says they mean the same thing.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say you should be careful with first name and last name?
comprehension.a: Because they mean the position on an English form, not the order you normally say your name in.
comprehension.why: This is the trap the text is written to prevent. Somebody who says their family name first will put it in the wrong box.

comprehension.q: According to the text, why do forms ask for capital letters?
comprehension.a: So the name can be read correctly and entered into a computer correctly, so letters arrive.
comprehension.why: The text says it is not about politeness and gives the real reason — a badly written name means the letter never arrives.

comprehension.q: What day and date is the appointment, and what time?
comprehension.why: All three are on the same two lines of the card. Say the date aloud as the fourteenth of March.

comprehension.q: What time should you actually arrive, and why?
comprehension.a: At 09:30, because the card says to arrive ten minutes before the appointment time.
comprehension.why: The arrival time is not printed — you have to work it out from 09:40 and the instruction below it. That subtraction is the whole point of the question.

comprehension.q: You cannot go. What must you do, and how long before?
comprehension.a: Telephone 0300 118 4422 at least 24 hours before, and then there is no charge.
comprehension.why: Both the deadline and the consequence are in the same short paragraph. Missing the 24 hours is what costs money.

grammar.title: Am, is, are: the verb you cannot avoid
grammar.explanation: Be is the most used verb in English. In the present it has three forms, and which one you use depends only on who or what the sentence is about. Many languages need no word here at all — English always does.
grammar.rule:
I am          We are
You are       You are
He is         They are
She is
It is

Negative: add not.  I am not. She is not.
Question: swap the first two words.  Are you ready?  Is she here?

Short forms: I'm, you're, he's, she's, it's, we're, they're.
grammar.workedExample:
Make a question from: She is from the north.
1. Find the two words at the front: She · is.
2. Swap them: Is · she.
3. Keep the rest exactly as it was: from the north.
4. Change the full stop to a question mark.
Result: Is she from the north?
Nothing else moves. This works for every sentence with am, is or are.
grammar.mistake: The commonest error at this level is leaving the verb out — I teacher, She tired, He from the north. Those are complete sentences in many languages, so it is not carelessness. English simply needs the word: I am a teacher. She is tired. He is from the north.
grammar.tip: Am belongs to I and to nothing else in the language.
grammar.practice:
Write am, is or are.
1. I ____ from a small town.
2. She ____ my neighbour.
3. They ____ at the office.
4. You ____ late.
5. It ____ my birthday today.
6. We ____ ready.
Now make numbers 2 and 4 into questions.
grammar.answers:
1. am  2. is  3. are  4. are  5. is  6. are
Questions: Is she my neighbour?  Are you late?
If you wrote is for number 3, check who the sentence is about — they is more than one, so it takes are.

grammar.title: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
grammar.explanation: These seven words replace the name of the person or thing you are talking about. English uses he and she only for people, and it for everything else — objects, places, animals, the weather, the time.
grammar.rule:
one person speaking .... I
the person you speak to  you
a man ................... he
a woman ................. she
a thing, place, animal .. it
you and others .......... we
other people or things .. they

I is always a capital letter, anywhere in the sentence.
You is the same word for one person and for many.
grammar.workedExample:
Replace the underlined words with a pronoun: <u>Ana and Tomas</u> are in the office.
1. Ask: is this one or more than one? More than one.
2. Ask: is it me, or the person I am speaking to, or others? Others.
3. More than one, others → they.
Result: They are in the office.
Notice are did not change. The pronoun and the verb form have to agree, and both were already plural.
grammar.mistake: Using he or she for a thing — the bus, he is late. In English a bus is it. This is not a serious error and people understand you, but it is one of the quickest to fix.
grammar.practice:
Replace the underlined words with a pronoun.
1. <u>My neighbour</u> (a woman) has a key.
2. <u>The office</u> is closed.
3. <u>Tomas and I</u> are colleagues.
4. <u>The forms</u> are on the desk.
5. <u>Dr Bennett</u> (a man) is in Room 3.
grammar.answers:
1. She  2. It  3. We  4. They  5. He
Number 3 catches people: when you are one of the group, the pronoun is we, not they.

grammar.title: My, your, his, her
grammar.explanation: These words say who something belongs to. They go in front of the thing, and they never change — not for a plural, not for anything.
grammar.rule:
I    → my      my name, my children
you  → your    your address
he   → his     his phone
she  → her     her office
we   → our     our class
they → their   their forms

Always before the noun.
Never changes for plural: my child, my children.
grammar.workedExample:
Whose phone? The phone belongs to Ana.
1. Ana is one woman.
2. The word for one woman is she.
3. She becomes her.
4. Put it in front of the thing: her phone.
Result: her phone.
Now the trap: it stays her phone even though a phone is not a woman. The word follows the OWNER, never the thing owned.
grammar.mistake: Choosing his or her to match the object instead of the owner — Ana and his phone. Ask who owns it, not what it is. If a woman owns it, it is her, whatever the thing is.
grammar.practice:
Write my, your, his or her.
1. Ana forgot ____ card. (Ana is a woman)
2. Tomas is looking for ____ keys. (Tomas is a man)
3. I cannot find ____ form.
4. What is ____ name? (asking someone)
5. The doctor is in ____ room. (Dr Bennett is a man)
grammar.answers:
1. her  2. his  3. my  4. your  5. his
Number 2 is the one to check: keys is plural, but the word stays his. These words never change for plural.

grammar.title: Numbers, and how old you are
grammar.explanation: English builds most numbers from a small set of parts, and it asks about age with the verb be — not with have, which is what many languages use.
grammar.rule:
13–19 end in -teen:  thirteen, fourteen … nineteen
20–90 end in -ty:    twenty, thirty, forty … ninety
Between: twenty-one, thirty-four, sixty-seven (with a hyphen)
100: a hundred or one hundred — never just hundred

How old are you?  →  I am thirty.
NOT: I have thirty.
grammar.workedExample:
Say the number 47.
1. Split it: 40 and 7.
2. The tens word: forty. (Note the spelling — four, but forty.)
3. The units word: seven.
4. Join with a hyphen: forty-seven.
Now use it for an age: I am forty-seven. Or in full: I am forty-seven years old.
Both are correct. The short one is what people actually say.
grammar.mistake: Two things catch people. First, saying I have thirty for your age — English uses am. Second, mixing up the -teen and -ty numbers: thirteen and thirty, fourteen and forty. The -teen ones put the stress at the end, and the -ty ones at the beginning.
grammar.tip: Age takes am, is or are — the same verb as everything else in this unit.
grammar.practice:
Write these in words.
1. 15
2. 50
3. 34
4. 82
5. 100
Then answer: How old are you? Write a full sentence.
grammar.answers:
1. fifteen  2. fifty  3. thirty-four  4. eighty-two  5. a hundred (or one hundred)
Your own answer should look like: I am ____ years old. If you wrote I have, change it to I am — that is the error this card exists to prevent.

grammar.title: Days, months and dates
grammar.explanation: Days and months always take a capital letter in English, wherever they appear. And a date is said differently from the way it is written — two small words appear when you speak it.
grammar.rule:
Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday
January February March April May June
July August September October November December

Always a capital letter. Always.

Written: 14 March    Said: the fourteenth of March
Written: 3 June      Said: the third of June

on Monday · in March · on 14 March
grammar.workedExample:
Read this out loud: 21 September.
1. The number is 21. For a date, use the ordinal: twenty-first.
2. Put the in front: the twenty-first.
3. Add of before the month: the twenty-first of September.
Result: the twenty-first of September.
The words the and of are not written on the page, but you say them. That is the part learners leave out.
grammar.mistake: Writing days and months with a small letter — monday, march. Many languages do not capitalise them, so this is a spelling habit rather than a mistake about English. It is also one of the fastest things to fix.
grammar.tip: Say the … of, even though neither word is written down.
grammar.practice:
Write these dates as you would say them.
1. 2 May
2. 14 March
3. 31 October
Then correct these sentences.
4. I start on monday.
5. My birthday is in june.
grammar.answers:
1. the second of May  2. the fourteenth of March  3. the thirty-first of October
4. I start on Monday.  5. My birthday is in June.
If you missed the capital letters in 4 and 5, that is the most common error on this card — go back and check every day and month you have written in this unit.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Seven sentences, seven pronouns
speaking.instructions:
Say these seven out loud, then again without looking.
I am here.
You are late.
He is my colleague.
She is my neighbour.
It is my birthday.
We are ready.
They are outside.
Record all seven. Play it back and check that you said am, is or are in every single one — the test is whether any sentence came out without the verb.
speaking.tutor: Say all seven to the tutor and ask whether the verb was there every time.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Introduce yourself in thirty seconds
speaking.instructions:
Say five things about yourself, in this order:
your name · your age · where you are from · where you live now · what you do
You may invent any of it.
Record it. Play it back and count how many sentences used am or is. It should be five out of five.
Then say it again, faster, without stopping between the sentences.
speaking.tutor: Give your five sentences to the tutor and ask it to say them back as though describing you to someone else.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — How old are you?
speaking.instructions:
Practise both sides of this exchange.
A: How old are you?
B: I am thirty-four.
A: And how old is your daughter?
B: She is six.
Now change the numbers and the people five times. Use ages that need a hyphen: twenty-one, thirty-four, sixty-seven.
Record the last one. Listen for whether you said am, and whether the hyphenated numbers came out as one word.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor how old it is, and answer when it asks you.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Say the date
speaking.instructions:
Read each of these out loud as a full spoken date, with the and of.
2 May · 14 March · 21 September · 3 June · 31 October · 1 January
Record all six. Play it back and count how many times you said the and of.
If the count is less than six each, say them again more slowly — those two words are the whole exercise.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say three dates and write down what you hear, then check the spelling of the months.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Meeting someone, six turns
speaking.instructions:
Say both parts of this conversation, changing your voice for each.
A: Hello. Are you the new student?
B: Yes, I am. My name is ______.
A: Welcome. I am ______, I am a colleague of Dr Bennett.
B: Nice to meet you. Sorry — what is your name again?
A: ______. It is a difficult one.
B: Thank you. See you tomorrow.
Record the whole thing. Play it back and check you used please, sorry or thank you at least twice.
speaking.tutor: Take part B and let the tutor take part A. Then swap and do it again.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Your details, out loud, unprepared
speaking.instructions:
Imagine someone at a desk is filling in a form about you and asking the questions.
Answer these out loud, without writing anything first:
What is your surname? · What is your first name? · How do you spell that? · What is your date of birth? · How old are you? · What is your address? · What is your phone number?
Record it. Listen back. Then do it once more and keep the second recording.
You may invent every answer — the point is the sentences, not the facts.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the person at the desk and ask you the seven questions in a different order.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Introduce three people
writing.prompt:
Write three short introductions, like the ones in Reading 1.
One for yourself, and two for people you invent.
Each one must be four to six sentences and must use am, is or are in every sentence.
Underline the verb in each sentence when you have finished.
writing.model:
My name is Ana Costa. I am thirty-four. I am from a small town in the north, but I live here now. I am a nurse. My English is not good yet, but it is better than last year.
This is Tomas. He is twenty-nine and he is a driver. His family is not here. His daughter is six and she is at school.
This is Priya. She is an engineer. She is from a city, but her parents are from a village. She is forty-one.
writing.length: Three introductions, four to six sentences each
writing.criteria: Three introductions; every sentence contains am, is or are; the verb underlined in each; the second and third use he/she and his/her correctly throughout; every sentence starts with a capital and ends with a full stop
writing.support: Do not write your own first — copy the shape of the second paragraph in the model and change the details. The structure is the hard part, not the facts.
writing.extension: Write a fourth introduction for two people together, so every sentence has to use are and their.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Whose is it?
writing.prompt:
Write eight sentences saying who things belong to.
Use my, your, his and her at least once each.
Underline the possessive word in every sentence.
Then check each one against the question: does the word match the OWNER, or did I match it to the thing?
writing.model:
1. My address is on the form.
2. Ana forgot her card.
3. Tomas cannot find his keys.
4. What is your phone number?
5. Her office is on the second floor.
6. His appointment is on Tuesday.
7. My family is not here.
8. Is this your surname or your first name?
writing.criteria: Eight sentences; my, your, his and her each used at least once; the possessive underlined in every one; every possessive matches its owner, not the object; every sentence complete
writing.support: Write the owner in brackets after each sentence while you work — (Ana, woman), (Tomas, man). Cross the brackets out at the end. Seeing the owner written down is what stops the error.
writing.extension: Add four more using our and their.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Fill in the appointment card
writing.prompt:
Look at the appointment card in Reading 3.
Write out a new card for yourself, with the same eleven lines, for an appointment next month.
Write the date in the written form (14 March), then underneath write how you would SAY it.
Work out and write the time you should actually arrive.
writing.model:
HEALTH CENTRE — APPOINTMENT CARD
Name: T. NOVAK
Patient no.: 5528 401
Appointment: Thursday 9 April
Time: 14:20
With: Dr Adeyemi, Room 7
Said aloud: Thursday the ninth of April, at twenty past two.
I should arrive at: 14:10
writing.length: A full card, plus two extra lines
writing.criteria: All the lines of the original card present; the day and month capitalised; the spoken form includes the and of; the arrival time is ten minutes before the appointment time and is correct
writing.support: Copy the card line by line first, with the details blank. Fill it in afterwards. A form is easier to complete than to design.
writing.extension: Write one sentence saying what you would do if you could not attend, using the information on the original card.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the seven mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence below has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each sentence out correctly.
Then write, next to each, which of the five patterns it came from.
1. I teacher.
2. She are my neighbour.
3. Ana forgot his card.
4. I have thirty-four.
5. My birthday is in june.
6. The bus, he is late.
7. Is your name what?
writing.model:
1. I am a teacher. (Pattern 1 — the verb was missing)
2. She is my neighbour. (Pattern 1 — wrong form of be)
3. Ana forgot her card. (Pattern 3 — possessive matched the thing, not the owner)
4. I am thirty-four. (Pattern 4 — age takes be, not have)
5. My birthday is in June. (Pattern 5 — months take a capital letter)
6. The bus is late. (Pattern 2 — a bus is it, not he)
7. What is your name? (Pattern 1 — question word first, then swap the two words)
writing.criteria: All seven corrected; each labelled with the right pattern number; no new mistakes introduced in the corrections
writing.support: Do the labelling first, before you correct anything. Once you know which pattern it is, the card for that pattern tells you the fix.
writing.extension: Write three more wrong sentences of your own, put them away for a day, then come back and correct them.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Am, is or are
activities.instructions:
Write am, is or are in each gap.
1. I ____ from another country.
2. My colleague ____ very helpful.
3. They ____ in the waiting room.
4. You ____ next.
5. It ____ my first day.
6. We ____ both students.
7. The forms ____ on the desk.
8. She ____ not here today.
9. ____ you ready?
10. My family ____ a long way away.
activities.answers:
1. am  2. is  3. are  4. are  5. is  6. are  7. are  8. is  9. Are  10. is
Two to check. Number 7: forms is plural, so it takes are. Number 10: family looks like many people but English treats it as one thing, so it takes is.
Eight or more correct means this pattern is working. Below eight, read the Pattern 1 card again and redo the exercise before moving on.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Replace with a pronoun
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each sentence, replacing the underlined words with I, you, he, she, it, we or they.
1. <u>Ana</u> is a nurse.
2. <u>The office</u> opens at nine.
3. <u>Tomas and Priya</u> are colleagues.
4. <u>My brother</u> is a driver.
5. <u>Priya and I</u> are in the same class.
6. <u>The appointment cards</u> are ready.
7. <u>Dr Bennett</u> is in Room 3.
8. <u>The bus</u> is late again.
9. <u>My neighbours</u> are very quiet.
10. <u>My birthday</u> is in June.
activities.answers:
1. She  2. It  3. They  4. He  5. We  6. They  7. He  8. It  9. They  10. It
The two that catch people: number 5, where you are part of the group so it is we and not they; and numbers 2, 8 and 10, where the subject is a thing, a vehicle and a day — all of them it.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Whose?
activities.instructions:
Choose my, your, his or her.
1. Ana cannot find ____ keys. (Ana — a woman)
2. Tomas showed me ____ appointment card. (Tomas — a man)
3. I have lost ____ form.
4. Excuse me, what is ____ surname? (asking someone)
5. The doctor is in ____ office. (Dr Bennett — a man)
6. She wrote ____ address in capital letters. (a woman)
7. Is this ____ phone or mine? (asking someone)
8. My neighbour parked ____ car outside. (a man)
activities.answers:
1. her  2. his  3. my  4. your  5. his  6. her  7. your  8. his
Every one of these follows the same test: ask who owns it, never what it is. Number 1 is the trap — keys is plural, but the word stays her. These words never change for plural.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Numbers, said and written
activities.instructions:
Part A. Write these in words.
13 · 30 · 15 · 50 · 18 · 80 · 44 · 67 · 91 · 100
Part B. Record yourself saying all ten in a mixed order. Wait ten minutes, play it back, and write down what you hear. Compare with Part A.
activities.answers:
Part A: thirteen · thirty · fifteen · fifty · eighteen · eighty · forty-four · sixty-seven · ninety-one · a hundred.
Watch the spelling of forty — no u, even though four has one.
Part B: the -teen and -ty pairs are the ones that go wrong, because they differ mainly in where the stress falls. If you confused thirteen and thirty on the playback, say them again with the stress exaggerated: thirTEEN, THIRty.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Dates
activities.instructions:
Part A. Write how you would SAY each of these.
1. 2 May
2. 14 March
3. 21 September
4. 3 June
5. 31 October
Part B. Correct these five sentences.
6. I start on tuesday.
7. My birthday is in august.
8. The appointment is on 9 april.
9. See you on friday the twelfth.
10. She was born in december.
activities.answers:
Part A: 1. the second of May  2. the fourteenth of March  3. the twenty-first of September  4. the third of June  5. the thirty-first of October.
Part B: 6. Tuesday  7. August  8. April  9. Friday  10. December — all of them simply need a capital letter.
If every one of Part B was wrong, that is normal: many languages do not capitalise days and months, so it is a habit rather than a misunderstanding. Now go back through everything you have written in this unit and check.

activities.title: Practice 6 — What do you say?
activities.instructions:
Match each situation to what you would say.
Situations:
a) You want to get past someone.
b) Someone thanks you.
c) You did not hear what someone said.
d) You arrive somewhere for the first time.
e) You are leaving.
f) You want someone to do something for you.
What you say:
1. Sorry — can you say that again?
2. You are welcome.
3. Goodbye.
4. Excuse me.
5. Hello.
6. Please.
activities.answers:
a-4 · b-2 · c-1 · d-5 · e-3 · f-6.
One to notice: a and c can both start with sorry in real speech — sorry, can I get past is perfectly normal. Excuse me is a little more polite for getting past, and sorry is the usual one for not hearing. Either will be understood.

quizzes.q: Which form of be goes with I?
quizzes.why: Am goes with I and with nothing else in the language. Is takes he, she and it; are takes you, we and they.

quizzes.q: Complete: My colleagues ____ in the office.
quizzes.why: Colleagues is more than one, so it takes are. Is would be right for a single colleague.
English needs both the verb is and the article a here. Leaving out either one is the most common error at this level.

quizzes.q: Replace the underlined words: Tomas and I are colleagues.
quizzes.why: When you are part of the group, the pronoun is we. They would be right only if you were not one of them.
English uses he and she only for people. A bus, an office, a city and a date are all it.

quizzes.q: Ana forgot ____ card. Which word is correct?
quizzes.why: The word follows the owner, not the object. Ana is a woman, so it is her card — whatever the object happens to be.

quizzes.q: Tomas cannot find ____ keys. Which word is correct?
quizzes.why: Tomas is a man, so it is his. Keys being plural changes nothing — these words never change for plural.

quizzes.q: How do you answer: How old are you?
options: My age is thirty years old.
quizzes.why: English uses be for age. I am thirty years old is also correct, but I am thirty is what people actually say. I have thirty uses the verb many other languages use here.
Forty has no u, even though four does, and numbers between twenty and a hundred take a hyphen.

quizzes.q: How do you SAY the written date 14 March?
quizzes.why: Two words appear when you say a date that are not written on the page: the and of. The number also becomes an ordinal.

options: I start on monday in march.
I start on Monday in march.
I start on monday in March.
I start on Monday in March.
quizzes.a: I start on Monday in March.
quizzes.why: Days and months always take a capital letter in English, wherever they appear in the sentence. Both words need one.

quizzes.q: Someone thanks you. What do you say?
quizzes.why: You are welcome is the standard reply to thank you. Excuse me gets attention, please softens a request, and sorry apologises — none of them answers a thank you.

teacherNotes.note: The course is designed for self-access. Every pattern card carries a worked example before its practice, every exercise has its answer key, and the Answers section gathers them in one place. If you are running this with a group, everything below is an accelerator rather than a repair.

teacherNotes.type: The one error worth your whole correction budget
teacherNotes.note: Omitting the verb be — I teacher, She tired, He from the north. Learners whose first language needs no copula produce these as complete, correct-feeling sentences, so treating it as carelessness will confuse them. Name it as a difference between languages rather than an error, and it usually fixes within a fortnight. Everything else in this unit is cosmetic by comparison.

Two things take longer than they look. First, the -teen and -ty number pairs, which differ mainly in stress and are genuinely hard to hear. Second, capitalising days and months, which is a writing habit rather than a misunderstanding and needs repeated small corrections across several units rather than one explanation here.

Reading 2 exists because the surname box causes real problems for anyone whose naming convention puts the family name first. Learners often fill it in confidently and wrongly. If you have a group, it is worth five minutes of comparing how names work across the room — but note the reading is written to stand alone for a learner who has nobody to compare with.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and no task here is scored by it alone. Learners must not be asked to give the tutor personal, immigration, medical or financial details. Every task in this unit says explicitly that details may be invented, and that wording should not be removed.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say who I am and where I am from, in full sentences.
I can choose he, she, it or they correctly.
I can use my, your, his and her without mixing them up.
I can ask someone's age and answer when someone asks me.
I can read a date on a card and say it out loud.
I can greet someone I do not know and end the conversation politely.

assignment.title: Your details, spoken and written
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record yourself answering the seven desk questions from Speaking 6 without notes: surname, first name, spelling, date of birth, age, address, phone number. Second, write out your own appointment card as in Writing 3, with the date written and also written as you would say it. You may invent every detail. Keep both together — the recording shows the spoken patterns and the card shows the written ones.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written card
